newsitem.title: FRANCE: New French government faces big economic challenge.
newsitem.headline: New French government faces big economic challenge.

text.p: French exports are booming but there is little other good economic news to cheer the party which wins this Sunday's runoff parliamentary election, economists said on Friday.

Unemployment is at a record 12.8 percent, growth is modest, domestic consumption is sluggish, consumer confidence is weak, social security spending is not under control and tax revenues may be lower than expected.
"We are at the start of a very slow recovery. The new government will be taking over an economy that will not be all that easy," said Societe Generale economist Michela Marcussen.

Economists say all this could mean France might overshoot the outgoing government's target of cutting the budget deficit to precisely 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year to comply with a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty.
The centre-right government, battling for re-election in the runoff vote, has insisted finances are under control and that it has no worries about the 1997 budget.
Economists say the government's decision to impose a budget freeze of an extra 10 billion francs should be enough to meet the central government budget deficit target of 285 billion francs.
The big problem could come in the welfare accounts. These could overshoot by 25 billion francs, said Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney.
This, he said, would imply a 3.3 percent public deficit in 1997. To avert this, the new government would need to raise social security contributions right away and cut hospital spending.

But both the Socialists and the centre-right now are stressing flexiblity on the criteria for a single currency in response to a public hostile to further sacrifice for monetary union. This means an overshoot of the targets could be possible.
Economists say the only area in which the economy is performing strongly is exports and that growth will come from foreign demand.

Official figures on Friday showed France had a seasonally adjusted trade surplus in March of 9.8 billion francs, bringing the total for the first three months of the year to 32.4 billion compared with 19.4 billion for the same period last year.
"It will be a foreign-demand led recovery... which will make the capital investment cycle start," said UBS economist Eric Muller who forecast 2.5 percent growth in 1997.
But this has not been reflected in business confidence. Figures this week showed expectations of future output weakening in May for the third straight month.
Private consumption is projected to be a weak 1.3 percent in 1997 compared with 2.1 percent in 1996. Unemployment is expected to peak in the next few months and then begin to edge downward.

If the Socialists win and introduce a less restrictive budget policy, growth could be higher than the official target of 2.3 percent, which the government has already said is too cautious, economists said.

"If they go for a push for growth, I would bump up my growth forecast from two-and-one-half percent to to perhaps two-and-three quarters," Sonja Gibbs of Nomura said. "What they really need to do is get consumers more confident."
